feedback.reason: The 120 ms request cannot wait for human review, but accepted high-risk work must be durable. Return pending only after durable queue admission and make capacity exhaustion explicit.
feedback.details: The boundary is synchronous durable acceptance followed by asynchronous review. Persist the case and stable identity before returning accepted/pending; then a worker may process it later. If persistence or bounded queue capacity is unavailable, do not claim acceptance. The response does not mean the fraud decision is complete. A transient broker handoff or in-memory queue is not enough evidence that the case will survive a restart.

messages.text: A best-effort handoff can disappear after success, violating the explicit durable-acceptance condition.
The caller deadline is for acceptance, not for the later human decision; waiting cannot meet the stated request boundary.
Process loss before the copy loses a case already reported as accepted.
Unbounded admission hides overload rather than applying explicit backpressure and can exhaust storage.

options.text: Durably enqueue the case before acknowledgment, then return a status ID for later analyst review.
Return success after publishing to a best-effort background channel and assume a consumer will recover dropped cases.
Keep the request open until an analyst completes the review, even when that takes longer than the 120 ms budget.
Acknowledge as soon as the process-local queue accepts the case, then copy it to durable storage when load falls.
Accept every high-risk case into an unlimited queue and never report overload to callers.

prompt: A high-risk fraud case must be reviewed later, but the API has a 120 ms response budget. The caller must not be told “accepted” unless the case survives process loss; queue saturation must be visible. What request boundary fits?

feedback.reason: The remote claim outlives the client deadline, so acceptance and confirmation must be distinct. A durable intent plus status lets retries resolve the same allocation without asserting success early.
feedback.details: Persist a stable allocation operation before returning pending. The inventory authority owns the atomic seat claim; only its committed result changes the operation to confirmed. A timeout or lost response leaves the same operation pending/unknown until a status read or reconciliation resolves it. Streaming progress may be added for convenience, but it does not replace a durable intent or safe retry identity.

messages.text: The claim may complete after the client deadline, so timeout does not prove it failed and a fresh retry may allocate twice.
Enqueue is acceptance, not reservation; a later rejection would invalidate a ticket already presented as confirmed.
A new identity hides the original uncertain attempt and can claim a second seat.
Disconnect loses the only status channel and cannot establish durable ownership of the allocation attempt.

options.text: Create one durable allocation intent and return its ID; resolve the seat asynchronously without resubmitting.
Wait synchronously for the remote inventory claim and treat a 300 ms timeout as a failed allocation.
Return confirmed as soon as the allocation message is enqueued, before the seat authority commits the claim.
Require each client retry to create a new intent so the allocator can restart from the beginning.
Stream allocator progress to the caller without persisting the intent or exposing a resumable status resource.

prompt: Ticket inventory allocation may take several seconds because seats are claimed from a remote authority. The client times out after 300 ms, but it must be able to learn whether its original seat request eventually succeeded. Which boundary is safest?

feedback.reason: The query is short and bounded, so a synchronous page fits the interactive use. Tenant authorization must occur before the data query; async work is justified only by an actual long-running case.
feedback.details: Authenticate the agent, authorize the tenant/case, then fetch at most 20 deterministically ordered messages in the same request. If the query later grows beyond the response budget, an async export can be introduced with a separately scoped authorization check. Queuing every ordinary read obscures a simple result, while querying before authorization or filtering in the client leaks data.

messages.text: The prompt gives a bounded interactive read that fits its budget; unconditional async work adds unnecessary delay and state.
Authorization after query already crosses the required tenant boundary and may expose protected records to logs or intermediaries.
Unbounded data access violates the requested bounded read and expands both cost and disclosure.
A one-time 80 ms read needs no subscription; the server must authorize the tenant independently of transport.

options.text: Return the bounded authorized page synchronously and propagate cancellation when the caller leaves.
Queue each case-history read as a durable job and make the agent poll even when the query normally finishes in 80 ms.
Read the 20 messages first, then check tenant membership before sending the response.
Return all history synchronously and let the client display only its latest 20 messages.
Open a long-lived event stream for a one-time history lookup and use the stream connection as authorization.

prompt: A support agent requests the last 20 messages for a case in their own tenant. The indexed history query completes in 80 ms; the endpoint must deny another tenant before reading its records. Which request boundary is appropriate?

feedback.reason: One bounded GET meets the stated read workload. Its response semantics—not asynchronous job creation—must distinguish freshness, confirmed absence, and unavailable dependencies.
feedback.details: Serve the lookup synchronously and attach an as-of timestamp or age. Return not-found only when the source confirms absence; label a lagging projection stale/not-yet-indexed and report source or projection failure as unavailable. This gives callers an honest result without making GET schedule work. A stream would fit a subscription, which the prompt explicitly excludes.

messages.text: The requested operation is a bounded read, and GET should not create ingestion work as an incidental side effect.
Projection lag is not proof that the authoritative asset is absent.
No subscription is requested; a bounded read needs a response, not a persistent connection.
That response hides a freshness-bound violation and conflates stale data with an available authoritative result.

options.text: Return metadata synchronously with its as-of state; preserve distinct missing and unavailable results.
Make GET enqueue metadata ingestion and immediately return a job-accepted response for every lookup.
Return 404 whenever the projection has no row, even if its watermark is behind recent source writes.
Open a long-lived stream for a single metadata read so later asset updates can be sent if they occur.
Return cached metadata with a normal success status even when the source is unavailable and its age exceeds 20 seconds.

prompt: A media client requests metadata for one asset. The projection may be 20 seconds stale; a confirmed absent asset is 404, while a projection or source outage is 503. The client is not subscribing to changes. What request boundary should serve this read?

feedback.reason: The device can be unavailable for hours, so caller wait and physical completion are separate. Durable async acceptance survives the offline period; deduplication belongs at the actuation effect owner.
feedback.details: Persist the command and stable identity before acknowledging acceptance. Deliver it when the device reconnects, and have the device/effect owner record processed command IDs so duplicate delivery does not repeat the unsafe action. Expose accepted, delivered, executed, and uncertain states distinctly. A transport acknowledgment proves only a message-handling step, not the physical outcome.

messages.text: A six-hour offline interval cannot fit a caller-bound synchronous request.
The device is offline and even delivery would not prove physical execution.
Fresh identities make repeated delivery look like new physical commands and bypass replay protection.
Queue acceptance is pending work, not proof of the physical side effect.

options.text: Durably accept the command while the device is offline and expose delivery/execution status by ID.
Keep the control request open until the device reconnects and physically executes the action.
Send the command over a stream and treat a transport write as proof the device acted.
Issue a fresh command ID on every reconnection attempt so the device can retry the action independently.
Return completed when the durable queue accepts the command, then let device execution happen later.

prompt: A command is accepted while an IoT device is offline and may not reconnect for six hours. The caller needs durable acceptance now and later execution status; replay must not repeat an unsafe physical action. Which boundary fits?

feedback.reason: Durable enqueue preserves the event beyond the initiating request. A bounded retry window contains load, while durable dead-letter and operator recovery prevent unacknowledged accepted work from disappearing.
feedback.details: Record the event and stable delivery ID durably before returning accepted. One worker owns up to 8 attempts over 24 hours with exponential backoff; if the partner never acknowledges durable acceptance, preserve the event in a durable dead-letter state and expose it for operator recovery. The receiver acknowledges only after persistence. This is at-least-once delivery within an explicit budget, not infinite retry or silent loss.

messages.text: The 10-second or offline dependency would hold request capacity and exceeds a normal caller-bound interaction.
A failure between response and persistence loses an event the sender promised to deliver.
A retry is the same event; changing its ID defeats receiver deduplication and can repeat the side effect.
Unlimited retries violate the 8-attempt/24-hour budget and can amplify an outage; after the bounded window, the event must remain recoverable in dead letter.

options.text: Durably enqueue one delivery; use eight attempts over 24 hours, then retain it in a recoverable dead-letter state.
Keep the original request open and retry the partner synchronously until it responds successfully.
Return accepted before the delivery event is durably recorded, then attempt to enqueue it in the background.
Assign a new event identity for every delivery attempt so the receiver can process every message independently.
Let the gateway and worker retry without an attempt budget or backoff while the partner is down.

prompt: A partner endpoint may be unavailable for hours. The sender may make at most 8 attempts over 24 hours; if none is durably acknowledged, the event must remain in a durable dead-letter state for operator recovery. What delivery boundary should the sender use?

feedback.reason: The update is bounded and the caller needs an immediate conflict result. A synchronous conditional write makes revision checking atomic with mutation; queuing or transport ordering cannot replace the precondition.
feedback.details: The document owner compares expectedRevision with the stored value in the same transaction that writes the content and increments the revision. One update commits; a later write still carrying 12 receives conflict and can reload or merge. An earlier read leaves a race window, and asynchronous work only changes when the conflict becomes visible.

messages.text: The requirement is a direct conflict result for a bounded write; asynchronous acceptance would hide that decision from the caller.
A competing edit can commit between check and write; the precondition must be atomic with the mutation.
This silently discards the first successful edit instead of returning the required stale-version conflict.
Transport order does not make the second client’s revision 12 precondition current.

options.text: Use compare-and-swap on expected revision so only one concurrent edit commits.
Queue both edits and return accepted before a worker later decides which version wins.
Read revision 12, check it in application code, then issue an unconditional write in a separate operation.
Accept the second write unconditionally and let the last request received overwrite revision 13.
Send writes over an ordered stream and assume arrival order means both are based on the current revision.

prompt: Two editors submit document writes against revision 12. The first commit should advance to revision 13; the second stale write must receive a conflict. The write transaction completes within 50 ms. What request boundary enforces the rule?

feedback.reason: Checkout needs a definitive answer and the last unit is contested. Synchronous response is appropriate because the bounded authoritative transaction can return its result; the atomic claim prevents double confirmation.
feedback.details: At the inventory owner, atomically require quantity greater than zero and decrement/claim it in the same transaction. Only the winning transaction returns confirmed; the other receives conflict or unavailable. A read before write is advisory, and queue acceptance is not reservation. If the system instead returns pending, it must delay confirmation until that same invariant commits.

messages.text: Confirmation precedes the authoritative claim, so both buyers can be promised the same unit.
Both buyers can read one remaining unit before either insert, then both write successfully.
Unary RPC does not serialize application state transitions or enforce the stock invariant.
Locks and caches are not shared across instances and do not guard the single authoritative stock record.

options.text: Claim stock atomically at the inventory owner before confirming either buyer.
Queue both reservations and immediately confirm each buyer; reconcile the inventory count after the workers run.
Check available quantity in a read, then create the reservation unconditionally based on that value.
Use unary RPC and assume the transport serializes concurrent requests to the inventory service.
Use an in-process lock around each API instance’s local quantity cache, then write reservations independently.

prompt: One stock unit remains and two buyers submit reserve requests concurrently. Each needs a definitive answer before checkout may show confirmation. Which request boundary preserves the inventory invariant?

feedback.reason: This is a small state-setting operation with immediate visibility. A synchronous idempotent set-state request avoids the cost and delay of an async job while making retries converge.
feedback.details: Bind the submission ID to the learner/module and set completion state rather than adding one on every request. A retry with the same identity returns the existing result; a genuinely new completion identity follows the domain’s separate rule. Keep GET read-only. Neither a stream nor a background job adds value for the short scalar update described.

messages.text: No long-running work is given; queueing introduces delay and state without a reason.
A lost response followed by retry can increment twice because the operation is not idempotent.
The operation is one scalar state change, not a continuous progress feed.
GET is repeatable and may be prefetched; a read must not perform the completion side effect.

options.text: Set the learner/module completion idempotently in the synchronous response.
Queue every completion as a background job and require polling even though the scalar update is immediate.
Expose incrementCompletion and ask the client to repeat it until it sees a response.
Keep a stream open for the one completion and treat each replayed message as another progress event.
Make GET mark the module complete when the caller refreshes its progress page.

prompt: A learner completes one module; the completion should be visible in the immediate response. The client can retry after a lost response, but retries must not increment progress again. What boundary fits?

feedback.reason: The write is short and publication success must mean revision 42 is authoritative. A synchronous conditional commit gives that meaning; cache invalidation is separate propagation work.
feedback.details: The price owner accepts only a revision greater than the current one and commits before returning success. Checkout must validate the authoritative revision or use a precondition so delayed cache invalidation cannot authorize revision 41. Notifications can accelerate propagation, but publication should not wait for every cache and a stream event is not the commit itself.

messages.text: The success response could precede the state checkout must validate, so revision 41 may still be confirmed.
A delayed old revision can overwrite the new price and violate monotonicity.
The authoritative write is short; tying success to every cache consumer makes publication depend on disconnected readers.
A stream notification may be delayed or missed; checkout must validate current revision at its decision point.

options.text: Commit the new authoritative price synchronously and publish cache invalidation separately.
Return success after queueing the price update, before the authority has committed revision 42.
Accept any update and let the last message received replace the current price, even if it carries revision 41.
Keep the publish request open until every checkout cache and instance acknowledges invalidation.
Broadcast a stream event and assume every checkout has received revision 42 before it can process a purchase.

prompt: A merchant publishes price revision 42. The authoritative write completes in 40 ms, while cache invalidation may take two seconds. Checkout must never confirm revision 41 after publish success. What request boundary should publication use?

feedback.reason: The endpoint’s success has a security meaning: old sessions must already fail at the relevant authorization checks. During propagation it must expose pending/uncertain, not success.
feedback.details: Track the revocation epoch and its enforcement progress. Until every path covered by the contract observes the new epoch, return pending or unavailable and reject requests when state cannot be safely established. Only then report success. Storing a request or queueing invalidation is not the same as enforcement; client cleanup and token expiry do not revoke sessions already held elsewhere.

messages.text: The API would report success while the old credential remains usable, contrary to the stated security guarantee.
The caller cannot know whether revocation is enforced, and propagation failure can leave sessions valid indefinitely.
The guarantee requires stopping old sessions, not merely waiting for their existing lifetime.
Other or offline clients still possess the old session and remain accepted by the server.

options.text: Report revocation success only after authorization checks enforce it; otherwise return pending.
Return success as soon as the revocation request is stored, although auth nodes may still accept old sessions for two seconds.
Queue invalidation messages and provide no status or indication of which enforcement nodes have applied them.
Do not invalidate auth checks; wait for every old token to reach its natural expiration and then report success.
Return success after instructing the user’s current device to clear its session, without changing server authorization checks.

prompt: Credential revocation must stop old sessions from authorizing new requests. Auth enforcement nodes may take two seconds to observe a new epoch. What should the revocation API return during that propagation window?

feedback.reason: A 25-minute task cannot share the 250 ms request lifetime. Durable acceptance and recoverable worker ownership let it outlive the request and any canceled polling connection.
feedback.details: Persist the job and ID before returning accepted. Workers hold leases so another worker can resume after replacement, while the job’s lifecycle remains independent of the client’s status request. Expose status by read-only lookup. Cancellation must be an explicit job command with its own semantics; closing a poll should only stop the caller from waiting.

messages.text: The request deadline is far shorter than the workload and should not control accepted job lifetime.
Worker replacement loses work that was already acknowledged.
A disconnected status channel does not imply the user canceled durable work.
Polling cannot recover an operation that was acknowledged but never durably recorded.

options.text: Accept a durable transcode job ID within the request deadline and keep processing independent of polling.
Hold the submission RPC open until the 25-minute transcode completes and let its deadline terminate the job.
Return accepted when a worker’s in-memory queue receives the task, then rely on that worker to finish.
Stream progress on the submission connection and terminate the transcode whenever the client disconnects.
Return a job ID before the durable job record is written and reconstruct missing work from client polling.

prompt: A video transcode normally takes 25 minutes; the submission request has a 250 ms deadline. The job must survive worker replacement, and a client canceling its status poll must not cancel accepted work. What boundary should the API expose?

feedback.reason: Flag evaluation and data migration are different state changes. Rollback is safe only if the persisted representation remains readable by both versions during coexistence.
feedback.details: Use a compatible expand-and-contract sequence: introduce an optional field/default and readers that tolerate either shape, then enable the server-evaluated flag. Keep old data semantics available throughout the five-minute rollback window and the week of old-client coexistence. Any destructive cleanup occurs only after the old-reader window closes and has its own migration/rollback plan. Turning a flag off cannot reverse data already rewritten.

messages.text: A flag changes behavior, not persisted bytes; old clients can still fail after rollback.
The async migration can alter data while old readers remain active and is not automatically reversed by disabling the flag.
A stale client-side flag cannot coordinate persisted data shape or protect old readers.
The stated week of coexistence prohibits an all-at-once client cutover.

options.text: Roll back the flag while keeping stored records readable by both app versions.
Assume disabling the feature flag will automatically restore records already rewritten into the new incompatible schema.
Asynchronously rewrite all records to the new format, then enable the feature once the migration queue is empty.
Cache the flag in each client and let clients choose which schema to read without server compatibility guarantees.
Make the new field mandatory in one atomic cutover and require all old clients to stop before enabling the flag.

prompt: A rollout flag can be disabled within five minutes, but app versions coexist for a week and both read persisted records. A new schema field is being introduced. Which synchronous/asynchronous boundary keeps flag rollback from breaking old readers?

feedback.reason: The caller needs a definitive booking decision and the authoritative transaction fits the request. Atomic overlap enforcement at commit ensures no success is returned for a conflicting slot.
feedback.details: Use an exclusion constraint or serializable transaction at the resource owner so only one overlapping reservation commits. Confirm after that commit; the losing request receives conflict. A read-then-write race remains even if each client has an idempotency key, because the two keys represent distinct intents. Async handling would need an explicit pending result and still would require the same final atomic guard.

messages.text: The confirmation precedes the invariant check and can promise two users the same time range.
Concurrent requests can both read the slot as free and then commit overlapping rows.
The keys deduplicate each intent independently and do not enforce a resource-wide conflict rule.
Stream order does not make the database conflict check and reservation atomic across all writers.

options.text: Commit the booking only when an atomic guard proves the resource interval is free.
Queue both requests and return confirmed immediately, then resolve overlap conflicts in a background worker.
Read availability in each request and perform unconditional inserts based on the result.
Use separate stable idempotency keys and assume that prevents two different booking intents from overlapping.
Send both requests over a stream and assume the transport orders them before the database writes.

prompt: Two buyers request overlapping appointment ranges for one resource, and each must know whether the booking succeeded before receiving confirmation. The conflict check and reservation are a short bounded transaction. Which request boundary is correct?

feedback.reason: Index maintenance is asynchronous, while a query can return synchronously. A watermark makes the bounded lag observable and preserves the distinction between projection delay and source absence.
feedback.details: Keep source writes authoritative and update the index in the background. Each query reports the index’s applied watermark or age; when the requested source state is newer than that watermark, report stale/not-yet-indexed rather than permanent absence. A source-confirmed missing record can be 404. Making the whole query asynchronous or pretending the projection is current hides the actual consistency contract.

messages.text: The scenario permits asynchronous indexing and a 15-second lag; coupling all writes to every index is unnecessary and may fail unrelated writes.
A missing projection row during a known lag interval does not prove the source record is absent.
The required read is synchronous; only index maintenance is asynchronous in this scenario.
Without the watermark callers cannot assess whether the index is within the 15-second freshness limit.

options.text: Return search results synchronously with the index watermark; report a lagging index as stale rather than claiming the source record is absent.
Block every source write until all search indexes apply it, then assume a successful write means all queries are current.
Return permanent not-found whenever the synchronous index query has no hit, regardless of its applied watermark.
Queue each search query as a background job even though the API can return the current bounded result immediately.
Expose results without an applied watermark and let callers assume the latest source writes are present.

prompt: Source writes are immediate, but search indexing can lag by 15 seconds. The API must return search results synchronously and distinguish a lagging index from a missing source record. What request boundary should it use?

feedback.reason: The two workloads have different time horizons. Batch work should have durable but bounded async execution, while urgent requests retain an independent capacity budget.
feedback.details: Return a job identity for accepted batch work, apply CPU/cost limits and fair admission, and defer or reject new batches when the bounded budget is reached. Keep urgent dispatch on a protected short path with reserved workers/capacity. An async queue by itself does not provide isolation if both classes drain through the same pool; priority must be enforced before saturation.

messages.text: Minutes of work can occupy the capacity needed to meet the urgent 100 ms deadline.
Durability prevents loss but shared capacity still lets batch work starve dispatch.
A label cannot help if batch tasks already occupy all workers or the queue is unbounded.
Retries add load to the saturated path and do not isolate the heavy workload.

options.text: Reserve urgent routing capacity and admit batch recomputation as durable lower-priority work.
Run batch recomputation synchronously in the same request pool as urgent dispatch until each plan is finished.
Queue batch work durably but drain it through the same unreserved worker pool used by urgent requests.
Add a priority field to requests but provide no reserved capacity or bounded admission.
Retry each delayed urgent route at every timeout while batch saturation remains unchanged.

prompt: Urgent dispatch route choices must return within 100 ms. Batch route recomputation takes minutes and is allowed to wait, but must not consume urgent workers. How should the request boundary handle batch work?

feedback.reason: The provider can outlive the 300 ms caller budget and time out ambiguously. A durable stable intent lets the API return pending and reconcile one charge rather than asserting failure or starting another.
feedback.details: Bind the provider request to a durable payment intent before sending it, and reuse the same idempotency key and parameters for retries or queries. If the response is lost, expose pending/unknown and reconcile the same intent; do not create another charge until the first outcome is known. The caller response reports acceptance, not payment completion. A stream cannot remove the ambiguity of a lost provider response.

messages.text: The provider may have charged before the timeout, so a final failure can prompt a duplicate payment.
Each fresh identity can create another charge; a later refund is not a duplicate-prevention contract.
The client cannot query or safely retry the original operation if the response was lost.
The stream can disconnect during the ambiguous outcome and a reconnect with a new identity risks a second charge.

options.text: Keep the original payment intent pending and reconcile it before any new authorization.
Wait for the provider in the original request and mark the payment failed when 300 ms elapses.
Create a new provider charge identity after each timeout and let reconciliation refund duplicates later.
Queue the provider call and return accepted without storing a stable intent or exposing status.
Keep a stream open until the provider responds and treat a stream reconnect as a new authorization.

prompt: A payment provider may have accepted an authorization even though its response times out. The user-facing request lasts 300 ms; later reconciliation is allowed, but the customer must not be charged twice. What request boundary should the payment service expose?
